title: Assessment archetype — a reusable, parameterized item shape
description: Governs content/competence/items/archetypes/<id>.yaml. An archetype is an assessment SHAPE, not an item about a particular element: 'construct a budget containing a correlated pair', 'diagnose a defective certificate', 'defend a decision rule against a stated alternative'. It is bound to specific assessable units by an item binding, which supplies the element's own parameters and rubric. One archetype may serve twenty to fifty units, and that ratio is the only reason a 9096-unit item bank is finishable at all — see decision 36 in docs/00-context.md. Archetypes are expensive and few; bindings are cheap and many. Write accordingly: an archetype that can only ever serve one element is a binding wearing the wrong hat.

itemType.description:
Listed in the order the authoring playbook prefers them. multiple-choice is permitted ONLY for genuine terminology and convention checks; anything else expressed as MCQ is a defective item, because the candidate has the internet open.

`witnessed-performance` is the exception to everything above: the candidate is OBSERVED doing the work rather than answering a prompt about it. It is the only shape that can assess an element whose `demonstration` route is `equipment`, and it arrived late — every other value here serves a desk item, and the consequence was that the corpus's authored equipment-route elements could not be bound to anything at all. Found by authoring EC-04-005 and trying to bind it. See `witnessRequirement`, which replaces `lookupResistance` for this type.

kinds.description: Which element kinds this archetype may be bound to. The validator refuses a binding whose element kind is absent here, which is the mechanical guard against the commonest binding defect: attaching a knowledge-shaped archetype to a skill element, so the candidate explains the thing instead of doing it. Most archetypes serve exactly one kind. An archetype claiming all three is usually too generic to test anything specific.

levels.description: Proficiency levels this archetype can assess, normally a contiguous band. Difficulty is carried by the parameter ranges the binding supplies and by the rubric, not by a different item.

prompt.description: The candidate-facing prompt template. Parameter placeholders are written {{name}} and must every one of them be declared in `parameters`; the validator rejects an undeclared placeholder and an unused parameter alike.

parameters.description: The knobs a binding sets. Every candidate receives a different draw, which is what makes a shared answer key worthless and is the whole basis on which proctoring was abolished.

visibility.description: Whether the candidate sees this parameter. `prompt` parameters are rendered into the prompt text and must appear there as {{name}}. `generator` parameters shape the artifact the candidate is given — which defect is injected into a budget, how large it is — and MUST NOT appear in the prompt: naming the defect hands the candidate the answer. The validator enforces both directions, because each failure is silent in a different way. An unrendered prompt parameter varies nothing; a rendered generator parameter destroys the item while leaving it looking correct.

unit.description: SI or accepted unit for the drawn value. Recorded so the scorer can check units rather than only magnitude — a numerically right answer in the wrong unit is wrong.

constraint.description: A relationship this parameter must satisfy against others, stated for the human reviewer rather than evaluated here. Example: 'must exceed u_a so the correlated term dominates'. A draw that violates physical sense produces an item that is unfair rather than merely hard.

scoring.description: How a response becomes a result. Deterministic where the question genuinely has a right answer; rubric-scored by a credentialed reviewer where it does not. Human effort is concentrated where judgement is actually required.

method.description: hybrid: a numeric part auto-scored, a justification part rubric-scored. Common for judgment elements, where the arithmetic is checkable but the defence is the point.

toleranceBand.description: Accepted deviation for a deterministic result, and its basis. A tolerance band that merely encodes rounding is too tight; one that accepts a wrong method is worthless.

rubricRef.description: Path to the rubric, which the playbook requires to ship in the same commit as the item. Required by the validator whenever method is rubric or hybrid: an unrubricked judgment item cannot be scored consistently by two reviewers, and inter-rater reliability is what makes the credential survive an audit.

witnessRequirement.description:
REQUIRED for a `witnessed-performance` archetype, and the field most likely to get one rejected. State what the witness must OBSERVE that the finished record cannot show.

THIS REPLACES `lookupResistance` RATHER THAN JOINING IT, because the two answer the same question for different item types. On a desk item, integrity lives in the answer not being lookupable or pasteable into an assistant. On a witnessed item it lives in the witness — and asking an author to explain why moving a weight across a load receptor resists an AI assistant produces a sentence written to satisfy a validator. A required field that reliably attracts filler is worse than the silence it replaced.

WHAT MAKES A WITNESSED ITEM DEFENSIBLE is that the observation catches something the artifact does not. If everything the witness would see can be recovered from the record afterwards, the item does not need a witness — and the element probably did not need an equipment route either. Writing this sentence honestly is the check on both.

lookupResistance.description: REQUIRED, and the field most likely to get an archetype rejected. State why a competent person cannot answer this by looking it up or by pasting the prompt into an AI assistant. Every assessment here is open-resource and unproctored, so this sentence is where integrity actually lives — if it cannot be written convincingly, the archetype is defective and no amount of parameterization repairs it. 'The numbers differ per candidate' is NOT sufficient on its own: an AI assistant solves a novel arithmetic draw effortlessly. What resists is a task requiring the candidate's own judgement, their own data, or a defence of a choice the source material does not make for them.

citations.description: Clause-level references grounding the archetype's technical content. Not required here as it is on an element — the bound element carries the authoritative citation — but an archetype asserting a technical fact should say where it comes from.

exposureLimit.description: Maximum times this archetype may be served to one candidate across all their bindings, before the bank must offer a different shape. Guards against a candidate meeting the same shape at every level of every element and learning the archetype rather than the competence.

authoring.description: Provenance for the archetype itself: who wrote it, when, and when it was last reviewed.

allOf.$comment: Which unfakeable sentence an archetype owes depends on how it is delivered. A desk item's integrity rests on the answer not being lookupable; a witnessed item's rests on the witness. Requiring both would guarantee that one of them is filler.
